cards.title: Stop asking "dawai li?" every night
cards.body: It gets you a reflex "haan" and a little irritation. A two-minute call can check on medicines without sounding like a school monitor.

cards.title: Open with their day
cards.body: Ask what they ate, who called, what the neighbours are up to. Medicines slip naturally into a chat about dinner.

cards.title: Ask the specific question
cards.body: "Did you take the night BP tablet after dinner?" beats "sab dawai li?" Specific questions get honest answers.

cards.title: Ask them to check, not remember
cards.body: "Ek baar strip dekh lo?" Memory blurs one day into the next. The strip doesn't.

cards.title: Listen for the small stuff
cards.body: Dizzy, sleeping badly, stomach upset. Note it for the next doctor visit instead of trying to fix it on the call.

cards.title: Know when it's not small
cards.body: Chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, sudden weakness on one side or confusion is not a chat topic. Call 112 or get them to a hospital right away.

cards.title: End on something nice
cards.body: Finish with a plan for Sunday or a silly forward from the family group. They should look forward to the call, not dread it.

takeaway: Ask about their day, then one specific medicine question, and let the strip answer instead of memory.
share: Send this to the sibling who calls Mummy every night.
